query: W is attractive for plasma-facing divertor components because of its high melting point, thermal resistance, low sputtering yield, and low tritium retention, but its relatively high ductile-to-brittle transition temperature limits use. CuCrZr provides favorable thermal conductivity as a heat sink but has a narrow operating-temperature range and is susceptible to irradiation embrittlement, requiring an intermediate layer that transfers heat efficiently while keeping both materials within suitable temperature ranges. Earlier HEA studies reported elevated-temperature strength retention in MoNbTaW and MoNbTaVW, thermal stability in Mo6.6Nb6Ni80Ta1.4Ti6, and favorable combinations of strength and ductility in NbTaTiV, HfNbTaTiZr, and TiVNbTa. Nevertheless, HEA performance can involve tradeoffs among strength, ductility, thermal stability, and phase constitution. TiVNbTa in a single-phase BCC dendritic state combines about 800 MPa yield strength with approximately 40% strain, but its reported yield and compressive strengths at 1273 K are only 330 and 423 MPa, respectively, at 30% strain. Under the constraints of efficient W-to-CuCrZr heat transfer, high-temperature mechanical stability, and compatibility with the limited operating ranges of both adjoining materials, what single intervention could improve the TiVNbTa intermediate material? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted change relative to the reported TiVNbTa baseline, temperature and loading boundaries, supporting evidence from the prior HEA results, and a controlled experiment that would falsify both the performance prediction and the proposed mechanism.

cited_evidence.text: Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are a relatively new class of multicomponent materials that are based on several refractory metals, but may also contain other, generally low density, elements and typically have a body centered cubic (BCC) crystal structure. These alloys have recently received much attention because of their attractive combination of properties not achievable by other classes of metallic alloys. For example, the first two RHEAs, NbMoTaW and NbMoTaVW, showed weak temperature dependence of yield strength in the temperature range from 600 °C to 1600 °C, with yield strength above 400 MPa at 1600 °C,. Unfortunately, these two alloys had high density (>12 g/cm3) and further developments aimed at reducing the alloy density while keeping superior high-temperature properties. In the second generation RHEAs, high-density Ta and W were replaced with lower density refractory elements, such as Cr, Mo, Nb, V and Zr, and low density Al and Ti were added. This resulted in RHEAs with lower densities and high-temperature strengths better than the properties of Ni-based superalloys and Fe-based steels. cited_evidence.text: Alloys of nominal compositions of NbTaTiV and CrMoNbV were synthesized, and in situ neutron-diffraction (ND) measurements were performed (Supplementary Notes 1 and 2, and Supplementary Fig. 1). The ND patterns show a single BCC solid solution at all temperatures up to 1,173 K (Figs. 2a and 3a). Atom probe tomography reveals NbTaTiV to contain 1.15 at.% (atomic percent) O and 0.45 at.% N, while CrMoNbV has low interstitial contents (0.083 at.% O, 0.034 at.% N, and 0.062 at.% C). The CrMoNbV also has an attractive density (ρ = 8.08 g/cm3) with a melting point of Tm ~ 2502 K and is studied in the as-cast state. Figure 1 shows the measured yield strengths (σy) versus temperature at a strain rate of 1 × 10−3 s−1; high strength is retained up to 1173 K (Supplementary Figs. 2 and 3). The strength of NbTaTiV is comparable to MoNbTaW and MoNbTaWV, which have been novel among BCC HEAs for their exceptional high-T strength retention, and have been predicted to be controlled by edge dislocations. Moreover, the CrMoNbV alloy has the highest reported strength at the homologous temperature of 1173 K.
